challenge.problemStatement: Given an employees table (employee_id, employee_name, department, salary), return every employee whose salary is among the top three distinct salary levels within their department. Ties at the third salary level must all be included.
challenge.theory: SQL analytical query exercise using aggregation and window functions.
requirements: Rank salaries within each department using DENSE_RANK; order results by department, salary descending, then employee_id.
constraints: SQL dialect: PostgreSQL unless a platform-specific adaptation is required.
Column names and schemas are specified in the statement.
hints: Write the base aggregation/deduplication CTE first.
Use a window function or grouped date arithmetic to identify ranks/streaks.
challenge.solution:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT employee_id, employee_name, department, salary,
         DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC) AS salary_rank
  FROM employees
)
SELECT employee_id, employee_name, department, salary
FROM ranked
WHERE salary_rank <= 3
ORDER BY department, salary DESC, employee_id;

challenge.problemStatement: Given orders(order_date, revenue), aggregate revenue by calendar month and return each month’s revenue, revenue from the same month one year earlier, and year-over-year fractional change. If the prior-year revenue is missing or zero, yoy_change is NULL.
challenge.theory: SQL analytical query exercise using aggregation and window functions.
requirements: Aggregate first by month, then use LAG(revenue, 12) across the ordered monthly series. Assumes a complete monthly calendar; insert zero-revenue months if the source omits months.
constraints: SQL dialect: PostgreSQL unless a platform-specific adaptation is required.
Column names and schemas are specified in the statement.
hints: Write the base aggregation/deduplication CTE first.
Use a window function or grouped date arithmetic to identify ranks/streaks.
challenge.solution:
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT date_trunc('month', order_date)::date AS month,
         SUM(revenue) AS revenue
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY date_trunc('month', order_date)::date
)
SELECT cur.month, cur.revenue, prev.revenue AS revenue_prev_year,
       CASE WHEN prev.revenue IS NULL OR prev.revenue = 0 THEN NULL
            ELSE (cur.revenue - prev.revenue) / prev.revenue END AS yoy_change
FROM monthly cur
LEFT JOIN monthly prev ON prev.month = (cur.month - INTERVAL '1 year')::date
ORDER BY cur.month;

problems.title: # First and Last Call to the Same Person

challenge.problemStatement: Given calls(caller_id, receiver_id, call_time), return one row for each directed caller/receiver pair with its earliest and latest call timestamps.
challenge.theory: SQL analytical query exercise using aggregation and window functions.
requirements: Use ROW_NUMBER in ascending and descending timestamp order to select the first and last call per pair.
constraints: SQL dialect: PostgreSQL unless a platform-specific adaptation is required.
Column names and schemas are specified in the statement.
hints: Write the base aggregation/deduplication CTE first.
Use a window function or grouped date arithmetic to identify ranks/streaks.
challenge.solution:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT caller_id, receiver_id, call_time,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY caller_id, receiver_id ORDER BY call_time) AS rn_first,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY caller_id, receiver_id ORDER BY call_time DESC) AS rn_last
  FROM calls
)
SELECT caller_id, receiver_id,
       MAX(CASE WHEN rn_first = 1 THEN call_time END) AS first_call,
       MAX(CASE WHEN rn_last = 1 THEN call_time END) AS last_call
FROM ranked
GROUP BY caller_id, receiver_id
ORDER BY caller_id, receiver_id;

problems.title: # Longest Daily Visit Streak per User

challenge.problemStatement: Given visits(user_id, visit_date), find each user’s longest streak of consecutive calendar days with at least one visit. Duplicate visits on the same day count as one day. Break ties by the earliest streak start.
challenge.theory: SQL analytical query exercise using aggregation and window functions.
requirements: Deduplicate user/day pairs, group consecutive dates using the gaps-and-islands row-number technique, then rank streaks.
constraints: SQL dialect: PostgreSQL unless a platform-specific adaptation is required.
Column names and schemas are specified in the statement.
hints: Write the base aggregation/deduplication CTE first.
Use a window function or grouped date arithmetic to identify ranks/streaks.
challenge.solution:
WITH days AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT user_id, visit_date::date AS visit_day
  FROM visits
), islands AS (
  SELECT user_id, visit_day,
         visit_day - (ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY visit_day))::int AS grp
  FROM days
), streaks AS (
  SELECT user_id, MIN(visit_day) AS streak_start, MAX(visit_day) AS streak_end,
         COUNT(*) AS streak_length
  FROM islands
  GROUP BY user_id, grp
), ranked AS (
  SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
    PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY streak_length DESC, streak_start
  ) AS rn
  FROM streaks
)
SELECT user_id, streak_start, streak_end, streak_length
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY user_id;
